# EVPI, EVPPI and EVSI: standalone R examples

Two self-contained value-of-information (VoI) examples, split front end /
back end:

- Front end — [decisionSupport](https://cran.r-project.org/package=decisionSupport):
  uncertain inputs are defined in `inputs/*.csv` as a 90%-confidence interval
  with a distribution shape (`estimate_read_csv()`); `mcSimulation()`
  propagates that uncertainty through the decision model to produce a Monte
  Carlo sample of inputs and payoffs.
- Back end — [voi](https://chjackson.github.io/voi/): `evpi()`, `evppi()` and
  `evsi()` compute the value-of-information measures from that sample using
  regression methods that work directly with continuous inputs.

This file is generated from [README.Rmd](README.Rmd); references come from
[bib/references.bib](bib/references.bib). Edit `README.Rmd`, not
`README.md`, and rebuild with
`Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render("README.Rmd")'`.

Install with `install.packages(c("decisionSupport", "voi"))`. Run with:

```r
source("examples.R")
source("tests.R")
```

This prints results and writes three CSVs plus a two-panel PDF to `outputs/`.

## What EVPI, EVPPI and EVSI mean

Choose the decision with the largest *expected* payoff, classical decision theory [@raiffa1961].

**EVPI** — how much better off we'd be, on average, if we could see every
uncertain input's true value before deciding, versus deciding now (e.g. "do
nothing").

**EVPPI** — the same idea for one input (or group), while the rest stay
uncertain; introduced to health-economic modelling by @felli1998. For example, learning 'yield' doesn't also reveal 'price', so we still need to average over the others before deciding. Inputs can also be individually worthless but jointly
decisive (example 2 below). `voi::evppi()` estimates this with a regression
fitted to the Monte Carlo sample [@strong2014].

**EVSI** — the value of one specific, realistic study that only partially
reduces uncertainty (e.g. a few trial plots), as opposed to perfect
information. It needs a model of how the study's data arise and update our
beliefs. `voi::evsi()` uses the regression method of @strong2015. A study
informing only one input is worth no more than perfect knowledge of that
input, which is worth no more than perfect knowledge of everything.

Net value of sampling is EVSI minus study cost: an expensive study can have
positive EVSI but negative net value. See @heath2017, @jackson2022, or the
book by @heath2024 for fuller treatments.

## Example 1: invest in an agricultural technology?

Yield and price are defined in
[inputs/investment_estimate.csv](inputs/investment_estimate.csv) as
independent positive-normal (`posnorm`) 90%-CIs:

| variable | distribution | lower (5%) | upper (95%) |
|----------|---------------|-----------:|------------:|
| yield    | posnorm       | 2          | 6           |
| price    | posnorm       | 20         | 40          |

```r
investment_estimate <- decisionSupport::estimate_read_csv("inputs/investment_estimate.csv")
investment_model <- function(x) {
  list(no_investment = rep(0, length(x$yield)),
       invest = x$yield * x$price - 100)
}
investment_mc <- decisionSupport::mcSimulation(
  estimate = investment_estimate, model_function = investment_model,
  numberOfModelRuns = 20000, functionSyntax = "data.frameNames"
)
voi::evpi(investment_mc$y)
voi::evppi(investment_mc$y, investment_mc$x, pars = list("yield", "price"))
```

`investment_mc$x`/`$y` are exactly the `inputs`/`outputs` `voi` expects.
Approximate results from 20,000 runs (varies slightly by run and method):

| Quantity | Currency units |
|----------|---------------:|
| Whole-model EVPI | ~8.7 |
| Yield EVPPI | ~6.6 |
| Price EVPPI | ~2.7 |
| Yield and price together, EVPPI | ~8.7 |

Yield captures most of the EVPI in our example model because payoff is close to linear in
yield over its range.

A pilot study measuring mean yield across `n` plots (known per-plot SD) uses
`voi`'s built-in `"normal_known"` design:

```r
voi::evsi(investment_mc$y, investment_mc$x, study = "normal_known",
          pars = "yield", n = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50), aux_pars = list(sd = 1.5))
```

Bigger pilots approach the yield EVPPI but never reveal price. Since larger
pilots cost more (`cost = 1 + 0.5 * n` here), EVSI minus cost turns negative
beyond a handful of plots, even as EVSI itself keeps rising.

## Example 2: complementary information

Neither of two variables alone changes the decision, but knowing both does.
Inputs (a rainfall anomaly and a pest-pressure anomaly, each normal with a
90% CI straddling zero) are in
[inputs/interaction_estimate.csv](inputs/interaction_estimate.csv). A new
crop variety is adopted only if there's a drought *or* a pest outbreak, not
both. This `xor` rule is a deliberately stylized worst case, chosen to have
*zero* marginal signal in either input alone, not a literal claim about how
adoption decisions work; a more realistic rule (e.g. also adopting when
both stresses hit at once) would soften the story below but not reverse it
— see the "general caveat" at the end of this section.

```r
interaction_model <- function(x) {
  drought <- x$rainfall_anomaly < 0
  pest_outbreak <- x$pest_pressure_anomaly > 0
  list(keep_old_variety = rep(0, length(x$rainfall_anomaly)),
       adopt_new_variety = ifelse(xor(drought, pest_outbreak), 100, -100))
}
```

By construction, whole-model EVPI is exactly 50, and each variable's own
EVPPI is exactly 0, but together it's also 50: worthless alone, decisive
together. Single-variable estimates from `voi::evppi()` recover the
near-zero values easily, but the *joint* EVPPI is a stress test, since there
is no additive signal for a regression smoother, only a pure interaction:

| Method | Joint EVPPI (true value: 50) |
|--------|------------------------------:|
| `"gam"` (default) | ~32, underestimates substantially |
| `"earth"` (MARS) | ~0, misses the interaction completely |
| `"bart"` (regression trees) | ~47, closest of the three |

A general caveat: always check whether EVPPI/EVSI for a parameter group is
sensitive to the regression `method`, and prefer ones that capture
interactions (`"bart"`, `"gp"`, or a `"gam"` with an explicit interaction
term). A softer, more realistic version of this model (e.g. the variety is
still worth adopting when both stresses hit at once) would lower the
numbers above and let the additive methods partly succeed, since each input
would then carry some real marginal signal — but the two inputs would still
be individually far less informative than they are together.

## Other things to keep in mind

- Separate learnable parameter uncertainty from irreducible randomness (e.g.
  future weather): average over the latter before computing EVPI, or a
  clairvoyant forecast of random events gets valued as scientific knowledge.
- `voi`'s regression methods are approximate: cross-check more than one
  `method` before trusting a single number for a real decision.
- If inputs are correlated, pass that structure to `estimate_read_csv()`
  (see `?estimate_read_csv`) rather than sampling independently.

## Packages

- [decisionSupport](https://cran.r-project.org/package=decisionSupport)
  (front end) [@luedeling2025decisionsupport]: also has `chance_event()`
  (risky events), `vv()` (year-to-year variation) and `discount()`
  (discounting cash flows).
- [voi](https://chjackson.github.io/voi/) (back end) [@jackson2024voi]:
  EVPPI/EVSI methods include `"gam"`, `"gp"`, `"bart"`, `"earth"`, `"inla"`
  (EVPPI) and regression, `"is"`, `"mm"` (EVSI).
- [BCEA](https://gianluca.statistica.it/software/bcea/) and
[SAVI](https://github.com/Sheffield-Accelerated-VoI/SAVI) for
cost-effectiveness-analysis-style outputs or a web interface.
